newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Republicans suggest smaller budget bills.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Republicans suggest smaller budget bills.

text.p: Top House Republicans Wednesday repeated their commitment to cut taxes as part of any balanced budget deal, but suggested splitting the overall budget into smaller bills that could more easily move through Congress.

"The Republican party continues to stand for lower taxes for all Americans. What we would really like to get done, ideally, is we'd like to take one major piece of this balanced budget and get it signed into law," Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich said after a closed meeting of House Republicans.
Kasich suggested working out a deal on Medicare spending.

Medicare was a major point of contention between Democrats and Republicans last year. The White House has recommended $106 billion in cuts in the health program over five years as part of President Clinton's balanced budget plan.
"It would be a terrific thing if we could in fact get the president to reach an agreement with us on saving Medicare," Kasich said.

Kasich and House Majority Whip Tom DeLay, a Texas Republican, said that Republicans were committed to a tax cut but were trying to figure out how to move procedurally. They would not say how big a tax cut they wanted.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich this week suggested delaying a tax cut until Congress finished work on a balanced budget pact. His comments sparked protest from conservatives in his party.
DeLay has also suggested putting off a tax cut. He told reporters, however, that Republicans want "as big a tax cut package as we can get." He said it was too early to talk about specific numbers.
Clinton has called congressional leaders to the White House for talks today aimed at reviving the stalled budget process.
"I don't have mood swings when it comes to the budget. I don't go up and I don't go down," Kasich said.
He said "the fire burns deep" in Republican souls for giving Americans a tax cut as part of a balanced budget pact.
Senate Republicans have called for about $200 billion in tax reductions over five years, about twice the level of tax breaks in Clinton's balanced budget plan.
